subject: Banking
title: Reserve Requirements
description: A short lesson to help you apply Reserve Requirements.

hook.text: Banks used to be required to keep 10% of deposits in reserve. In 2020, the Fed dropped that requirement to zero.

buildup.text: Reserve requirements limit how much banks can lend. Higher reserves mean less lending.

discovery.text: With zero reserves required, banks can theoretically lend every dollar deposited.

twist.text: China's central bank actively uses reserve ratios. It adjusts them to control lending in ways the Fed no longer does.

climax.text: Reserve requirements were banking's oldest control lever.

punchline.text: Reserve requirement: zero. The Fed now uses other tools to control banks.

quiz.question: What is the current US bank reserve requirement?

details.summary: Reserve requirements mandate how much cash banks must hold against deposits, limiting how much they can lend. This traditional tool has been largely replaced by capital requirements and interest rate policy in modern banking.
details.whyItMatters: Reserve requirements directly control the money multiplier effect. While less prominent today, understanding them reveals how central banks historically managed the money supply and banking system stability.
takeaways: The Fed reduced reserve requirements to zero in March 2020
Higher reserves limit bank lending, lower reserves encourage it
China's central bank still actively uses reserve ratios as a policy tool

faq.question: Why did the Fed set reserve requirements to zero?
faq.answer: Modern banking regulation uses capital requirements, stress tests, and liquidity coverage ratios to ensure bank safety. The Fed determined these tools were more effective than reserve requirements and eliminated them to simplify bank operations.

faq.question: How do reserve requirements affect lending?
faq.answer: If a bank must hold 10 percent of deposits in reserve, a $100 deposit can support only $90 in loans. At zero reserve requirements, the theoretical lending capacity is unlimited, though capital requirements still constrain actual lending.
